bib.title: Robustness and Fault Tolerance Patterns (ch. 7, Agentic Architectural Patterns for Building Multi-Agent Systems)

question: Which architectural patterns make a multi-agent LLM system resilient to accidental failures and malicious attacks, and in what order should a team adopt them?
contributions: A five-level robustness maturity model (Table 7.1) that orders the patterns for progressive adoption
A four-tier integration architecture (execution, orchestration, governance and observability, security and safety) and a loan-application chaining example
Seventeen patterns, each with context, problem, solution, worked example, Python sketch, consequences and guidance
A sample metrics table (Table 7.2) for measuring pattern effectiveness

results.claim: Recommended failure chain: adaptive retry, then auto-healing restart, then fallback model or redundant agent, then delayed escalation to a human, all logged in the causal dependency graph.
results.setup: Loan-application workflow with a central orchestrator (Fig 7.1); design recommendation, no measurement.
results.quote: All automated paths are exhausted → Delayed Escalation notifies a human operator for manual intervention.

results.claim: Five-level maturity model: L1 hardcoded chains with no patterns; L2 reactive recovery (Parallel Consensus, Watchdog, Adaptive Retry); L3 adaptive fault tolerance (Auto-Healing, Fallback Model, Checkpointing, Rate Limit, Delayed Escalation); L4 observable (Causal Graph, Trust Decay, Canary); L5 secure (Mesh Defense, Envelope Isolation, Majority Voting). Start at L2.
results.setup: Table 7.1; authors' recommended rollout, not validated empirically.
results.quote: Begin by implementing the Level 2 (reactive recovery) patterns to establish baseline stability with minimal architectural change.
results.note: Self-Defense, Translation Overhead (pass-by-reference) are not placed in any level of Table 7.1; Majority Voting is placed at L5 although its example is a loan decision.

results.claim: Worked example, invented: two credit agents return 720 and 725; difference 5 is under the 10-point tolerance, so the average 722.5 is accepted. A 720 vs 780 split would go to a human.
results.setup: Parallel Execution Consensus, PrimaryCreditAgent (Model A) and BackupCreditAgent (Model B), tolerance 10 points. Illustrative numbers, not measured.
results.quote: Resolution: The orchestrator validates the result and calculates the average score (722.5) as the final, trusted output.
results.note: The code simulates scores with random.randint(700, 750) and random.randint(705, 755).

results.claim: Worked example, invented: a compliance agent with 85% confidence is below the 95% auto-approve threshold, is retried twice, then escalated to a human with a case file.
results.setup: Delayed Escalation Strategy, ComplianceAgent, MAX_RETRIES = 2, 1 s sleep in code. Illustrative.
results.quote: ComplianceAgent goal: To analyze transactions and approve them only if the confidence score is above
results.note: The 95% appears on the next line of the text; the 85% figure is in 'its confidence score is only 85%, which'.

results.claim: Worked example, invented: a watchdog timer cancels a hanging analysis agent and fails over to a backup agent.
results.setup: Watchdog Timeout Supervisor, primary analysis agent hangs; backup agent does a simpler analysis.
results.quote: Simultaneously, the orchestrator starts a 10-second timer.
results.note: Inconsistent: prose says 10 seconds, the code sets TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 5 ('Set a 5-second timeout') with a 15 s primary sleep and 1 s backup sleep.

results.claim: Adaptive Retry mutates the prompt after a validation failure (rephrase, add examples, decompose via chain-of-thought, tighten constraints) instead of resending the same request.
results.setup: JSON entity extraction; the LLM is simulated, no real model run.
results.quote: Constraint tightening: Adding more specific constraints about the output format (e.g., Ensure your response is valid JSON).

results.claim: Auto-healing: a supervisor watches heartbeats and restarts crashed agents; the guidance is to add crash-loop backoff and to pair stateful agents with checkpointing.
results.setup: Supervisor sketch with a 10 s check interval and a simulated 20% failure rate.
results.note: Code also uses 'if random.random() < 0.2:  # 20% chance of appearing unhealthy'.

results.claim: Majority voting with three agents: two Approve and one Review gives a majority of 2 out of 3; a three-way split escalates to a human. Use an odd number of agents.
results.setup: Majority Voting Across Agents, loan decision, hard-coded agent outputs; majority is more than half.
results.quote: Final decision: The orchestrator determines that Approve has a clear majority (2 out of 3).

results.claim: Worked example, invented: causal graph for a denied loan has five nodes; Node 4 risk score 75 depends on validated data and an external credit report, and Node 5 Deny depends on Node 4.
results.setup: Causal Dependency Graph; code denies if risk_score > 50, external credit score 620.
results.quote: The RiskAssessmentAgent takes both app_data_validated (Node 2) and credit_report (Node 3) as input and produces a risk score of 75.
results.note: Quote is split across a line break in the text; the number 75 is in 'produces a risk score of 75'.

results.claim: Agent Self-Defense: sanitise untrusted input then wrap it in XML delimiters and tell the model to treat the tagged block as data; the authors concede it is not foolproof and is one layer among several.
results.setup: Feedback summariser; the LLM call is simulated, so the attack is never tested against a real model.

results.claim: Agent Mesh Defense: a firewall agent mediates every inter-agent message against allowed_senders policies; example blocks ChatbotAgent from querying CustomerDatabaseAgent. The code defaults to allow when no policy exists.
results.setup: Zero-trust, least-privilege access policy; simulation only.
results.quote: # Here, we default to allow if no policy is found.
results.note: Default-allow in the code contradicts the least-privilege guidance given in the same section.

results.claim: Sandboxing: run high-risk tool code in an isolated environment with network, filesystem and resource limits; a bare subprocess with a 5 s timeout is only a basic form and containers (Docker, Firecracker, gVisor) are recommended.
results.setup: SandboxedComputationAgent running python3 -c in a subprocess.
results.quote: # Run code in a subprocess with a 5-second timeout.
results.note: The subprocess does not block os.listdir('/'), so the sketch does not enforce the policy the prose describes.

results.claim: Worked example, invented: rate limiter for a credit bureau API capped at 100 requests per minute; a spike of 200 applications has the 101st request blocked.
results.setup: Rate-Limited Invocation, sliding window of 60 s over a deque of timestamps.

results.setup: Trust Decay and Scoring, three redundant summarisation agents.

results.note: Prose penalty is 0.1 (1.0 to 0.9) but the code uses failure_decrement = 0.2 and success_increment = 0.1 with a floor of 0.1. Also, no decay is implemented in the code despite the pattern name; 'Scoring up' increments only. Prose scoreboard: ({A: 1.1, B: 0.9, C: 0.9}).

results.claim: Canary Agent Testing in shadow mode sends a copy of each request to the new version and logs both outputs for offline comparison; later move to a live canary on a small share of traffic.
results.setup: SummarizationAgent v1 stable vs v2 canary; the 1% is given as an example only.
results.quote: a small percentage of user traffic (e.g., 1%) is routed to the canary
results.note: Shadow mode doubles infrastructure and inference cost during the test (stated in Cons).

limits: The chapter reports no experiments: every number is an invented illustration (credit scores, 95% confidence, 10 s timer, 100 requests per minute, trust scores) and every LLM call in the code is simulated.
Table 7.2 names metrics but gives no target values, thresholds or measured effect of any pattern on failure rate, cost or latency.
The maturity ordering (Table 7.1) is the authors' judgement and is not tested; some patterns (Self-Defense, Translation Overhead) are not placed in it.

Code sketches diverge from the prose: watchdog timeout 10 s vs 5 s, trust decrement 0.1 vs 0.2, no decay in the trust code, firewall default-allow, subprocess sandbox that does not block the filesystem listing, and a malformed '< user_review>;' tag in the self-defense sketch.
Prompt-injection defence rests on delimiters plus html.escape, which does not remove instruction-like text; authors say it is not foolproof and should be one layer.
Majority voting and parallel consensus assume agent errors are independent; the chapter advises different models or prompts but does not address correlated errors from a shared base model.
Package and tool names (ratelimiter, Neo4j, Neptune, Firecracker, gVisor, Redis) are suggestions and may have dated.
practices: Adopt the patterns progressively, starting with Level 2 reactive recovery, then Level 3, then Levels 4 and 5 (Strategic guide, p.207).
Define a tolerance for agreement and an escalation path (third tie-breaker agent, rule-based fallback or human) before using Parallel Execution Consensus (Parallel Execution Consensus, guidance).
Try automated recovery (retry, backup agent, other tool) first and send a human a full context packet only after a set number of attempts or time window (Delayed Escalation Strategy).
Tune the retry count, wait between attempts and escalation conditions to the use case, e.g. seconds for fraud detection and minutes for non-critical data processing (Delayed Escalation, guidance).
Wrap agent calls in a timeout using async frameworks and clean up cancelled tasks so locks are released (Watchdog Timeout, guidance).
Keep a library of prompt mutations per failure mode, starting with few high-impact ones such as stricter JSON instructions or step-by-step reasoning (Adaptive Retry, guidance).
Use heartbeat or /health checks with crash-loop backoff, and combine with checkpointing for stateful agents (Auto-Healing, guidance).
Place checkpoints after the most expensive or risky steps, make writes atomic, and use a durable store (Incremental Checkpointing, guidance).
Use an odd number of voting agents, as independent as possible (different foundation models, prompt templates or fine-tuning data), and define the no-majority protocol (Majority Voting, guidance).
Use a standard enforced logging schema for the causal graph, and a graph database for complex or frequently traversed graphs (Causal Dependency Graph, guidance).
Use strong non-natural delimiters, state their role in the system prompt, and combine with output validation and anomaly monitoring (Agent Self-Defense, guidance).
Apply least privilege to inter-agent access policies and make the firewall agent high-performance and highly available (Agent Mesh Defense, guidance).
Deny all sandbox permissions by default, grant the minimum, and prefer mature technology such as Docker over bare subprocesses (Execution Envelope Isolation, guidance).
Pass large payloads by reference through a shared store with a key naming convention and a TTL (Optimizing for Translation Overhead, guidance).
Use a tested rate-limit library and exponential backoff on rate-limited retries (Rate-Limited Invocation, guidance).
Keep primary and backup models behind separate prompt templates and output validators, and check both exceptions and invalid outputs (Fallback Model Invocation).
Guard against agent starvation in trust scoring by letting scores decay back toward a baseline (Trust Decay, Solution and Cons).
Start canary testing in shadow mode, then a small live share, and compare on business metrics as well as output similarity (Canary Agent Testing, guidance).
Measure each pattern with its metric because patterns add latency and token cost (Measuring robustness, Table 7.2).

terms.definition: Also known as Agent Failover to Agent; invokes two or more independent agents in parallel on the same task and compares outputs within a tolerance, escalating on disagreement.
A tiered escalation path that attempts automated recovery steps first and escalates to a human only after a predefined number of attempts or a time window, with a full context packet.
Wraps agent calls in a timed execution block; on timeout the supervisor cancels the task and triggers a fallback.
A retry that modifies the prompt after a failure (rephrase, add examples, decompose, tighten constraints) rather than resending it unchanged.
An external supervisor monitors agent health, often via heartbeat, and restarts crashed agent processes to a clean state.
Saves intermediate state to a durable store at key milestones so a restarted workflow resumes from the last successful step.
Three or more independent agents perform the same task and a majority vote decides; no clear majority escalates to a human.
A structured, machine-readable record of each step's inputs, data sources and outputs, traversable backward from any outcome.
Input sanitisation plus delimiter wrapping so the model treats untrusted input as data, not commands.
A zero-trust firewall agent that inspects every inter-agent message against access policies and blocks and logs violations, preventing lateral movement.
Runs high-risk agent tasks in an isolated runtime with predefined network, filesystem and resource limits to limit blast radius.
The time to formulate, serialise, send and process data between agents; reduced by storing payloads in a shared store and passing only a key.
Wraps tool calls with a limiter that keeps a log of recent request timestamps and queues, delays or rejects requests over the window limit.
Switches at runtime from a failing primary LLM (error, timeout or constraint violation) to a stable backup model.
The orchestrator keeps a numerical trust score per worker agent, raised on success, lowered on failure, decaying toward a baseline, and routes to the highest score.
An agent whose score has dropped so low it is never chosen again, even after its issue is fixed.
Deploys a new agent version alongside the stable one, sends it a copy of live requests in the background, and logs both outputs for offline comparison.
